title: Breath to the immortal air; this body ends in ashes
theme: The dying person’s words: the breath returns to the air, the body to ashes, and the mind is called on to remember what has been done.

words.role: subject of the first clause (with a verb to be supplied)
words.context: Śaṅkara: «वायुः प्राणः», the vital breath; Deśika: the self, called vāyu because it goes from body to body

words.gram: m. acc. sg. (or n. nom. sg.)
words.role: goal of the breath (Śaṅkara), or a predicate of the self (Deśika)
words.context: Deśika: «निलयनरहितत्वात् क्वचिदपि व्यवस्थितत्वाभावाच्च अनिलम्», ‘without abode’; Madhva: «अः ब्रह्मैव निलयनं यस्य वायोः सोऽनिलम्», ‘whose abode is a, that is Brahman’

words.gram: adj., m. acc. sg. (or n. nom. sg.)
words.role: qualifies anilam (Śaṅkara), or a further predicate (Deśika)

words.context: Deśika lists three senses: a change of subject, ‘after the self departs’, or ‘as everything subject to karma does’
Deśika: the word itself means ‘what falls apart’ («शरीरशब्दे व्युत्पत्तिनिमित्तानुसारेण विशरणस्वभावत्वं गम्यते»)

words.role: invocation that opens the second half
words.context: Śaṅkara: Om as the symbol of Brahman called Agni («ओम्प्रतीकात्मकत्वात्सत्यात्मकमग्न्याख्यं ब्रह्माभेदेनोच्यते»)

words.meaning: O resolve, O will; (or) O sacrifice
words.context: Śaṅkara: «हे क्रतो सङ्कल्पात्मक»; Deśika: «क्रतो - क्रत्वात्मक», ‘you who are the sacrifice’

words.gram: verb, root smṛ (1st class, P.), imperative 2nd sg.
words.context: Deśika: «स्मर - सानुग्रहया बुद्ध्या विषयीकुरु», ‘hold [me] in your gracious mind’

words.gram: past passive participle used as a noun, n. acc. sg.
words.context: Śaṅkara: «यन्मया बाल्यप्रभृत्यनुष्ठितं कर्म», ‘the works I have performed from childhood’

sandhi.rule: vāyuḥ: after u, a visarga that stands for s becomes r before a vowel (P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः)); anilam and amṛtam keep their m before a vowel; atha + idam: a + i → e, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).
P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः). The Saṃhitā witnesses write the nasal before ś as ँ (भस्मान्तँ शरीरम्).
bhasman loses its final n as the first member of a compound (bhasma-), and a + a → ā: bhasma + anta → bhasmānta.
P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः); written कृतँ स्मर in the Saṃhitā witnesses.

morphology.note: The first clause has no verb. Śaṅkara supplies one, ‘may [the breath] attain’: «सूत्रात्मानं प्रतिपद्यतामिति वाक्यशेषः», so that anilam amṛtam is its accusative goal: ‘[let my] breath [go to] the immortal air’. Mahīdhara supplies the same. Deśika takes vāyuḥ, anilam and amṛtam as three predicates of the pure self, with no verb supplied; then anilam and amṛtam are neuter nominatives.

The Saṃhitā witnesses write the syllable with the pluti figure, ओम्३ / ओ३म्, marking it as prolonged; the Upaniṣad witnesses write ॐ or ओं. The prolongation is a recitational feature and is not shown in the edition’s text.

Vocative of kratu, a word with a wide range in Vedic: will, resolve, intelligence, and the sacrifice. Śaṅkara takes the sense ‘resolve’ («सङ्कल्पात्मक»), Deśika the sense ‘sacrifice’ (with the Gītā’s ‘I am the kratu’) or, ‘from the context’, meditation.
Imperative of smṛ. The repetition is explained by Śaṅkara as showing earnestness («पुनर्वचनमादरार्थम्») and by Deśika as showing urgency («त्वरातिशयात्»).

anvaya: वायुः अमृतम् अनिलम् [प्रतिपद्यताम्] । अथ इदम् शरीरम् भस्मान्तम् [भूयात्] । ओम् क्रतो स्मर कृतम् स्मर क्रतो स्मर कृतम् स्मर ।
syntax: Two parts. The first is two nominal sentences without a finite verb: ‘breath — the immortal air’; ‘and this body — ending in ashes’. They can be completed as wishes (Śaṅkara: ‘may the breath attain the immortal air, may this body end in ashes’) or as statements about the self and the body (Deśika). The second part is a formula: Om, then a vocative (krato) and imperatives (smara) with an object (kṛtam), said twice. The anvaya follows Śaṅkara’s construction and marks his supplied verbs.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara and Mahīdhara: the vital breath of the dying, leaving its individual limits for the cosmic air, the ‘thread-self’ («अध्यात्मपरिच्छेदं हित्वा अधिदैवतात्मानं सर्वात्मकम् अनिलम् अमृतं सूत्रात्मानं»). Deśika: the pure self, called vāyu because it travels, anila because it has no fixed abode, amṛta because it does not die when the body does («अनन्तरं तु परिशुद्धात्मस्वरूपमुच्यते»). Madhva: vāyu is the deity Vāyu, immortal because his knowledge is never obscured; anila ‘whose abode is Brahman’.

ambiguities.topic: kratu: resolve, sacrifice, or the Lord
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the vocative addresses Om, the Brahman called Agni, as ‘you whose nature is resolve’. Deśika: the Lord in the form of the sacrifice, or (by context) meditation itself. Madhva’s cited verse makes kratu a name of Hari ‘because he is knowledge’ («स क्रतुर्ज्ञानरूपत्वादग्निरङ्गप्रणेतृतः»).

‘Remember what has been done.’ Śaṅkara: Agni (as kratu) is asked to remember the works the dying person has performed since childhood. Deśika: the Lord is asked to regard with grace whatever good the devotee has done — or what the Lord himself has done for him. The mantra does not say whose deeds are meant.

VS 40.15 reads ‘om krato smara | klibe smara | kṛtaṃ smara’. Mahīdhara takes klibe as a Vedic form of klṛp: ‘remember, for the world that is fashioned [for enjoyment]’. He also reports Kātyāyana’s rule that the yogin is reminded of his sacrifices at the end with these yajus («'क्रतो इत्यादि त्रिभिर्यजुर्भिरन्ते यज्ञान्योगी स्मारयति' ( अनु० ४ । ९) इति कात्यायनः»).
Madhva divides this mantra into two (his 18 and 19), and his text repeats Om before the second ‘krato smara’ (corrections.json, variant).

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Not a metrical verse: counted as written, 17 syllables in the first half and 16 in the second. Mahīdhara calls the Mādhyandina form ‘two yajus’ («द्वे यजुषी»), that is, prose formulas, and the second half is a ritual formula repeated.

translation.literal: Breath — the immortal air; then this body — ending in ashes. Om. O resolve, remember; what has been done, remember. O resolve, remember; what has been done, remember.
translation.readable: Let my breath go to the immortal air, and this body end in ashes. Om. Mind, remember; remember what was done. Mind, remember; remember what was done.

beginner: This verse is spoken at the edge of death. It is very plain. The breath, it says, goes back to the wind, which does not die; and this body ends as ashes, as every cremated body does. Nothing is softened. Then comes a call: ‘Remember! Remember what has been done!’ — said twice, the way someone repeats an urgent request. Who is asked to remember? Some teachers say it is the fire, or the divine, asked to remember the good the dying person has done; others say it is the person’s own mind, gathering itself at the last moment. The verse holds two things side by side without contradiction: the honest fact that the body ends, and the conviction that a life’s doing and intending still count.
analogy: It is like the last minutes before handing in an exam: the paper will be collected whatever happens, and in those minutes you gather everything you have learned into what you can still write.

commentary.q: What does the mantra say, before interpretation?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Two verbless statements — ‘breath, the immortal air’; ‘and this body, ending in ashes’ — followed by Om and a twice-repeated call: ‘O kratu, remember; remember what has been done’. The first half describes the elements of a person dissolving: breath into wind, body into ash. The second half addresses someone, called kratu, and asks for remembering. It is the third of the four closing prayers, and like the others it occurs in Bṛhadāraṇyaka 5.15.1.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara reads it as the words of the dying meditator: ‘now, as I am about to die’ («अथेदानीं मम मरिष्यतो»), the breath is to attain the immortal air, the subtle body, refined by knowledge and works, is to go out («लिङ्गं चेदं ज्ञानकर्मसंस्कृतमुत्क्रामत्विति द्रष्टव्यम्»), and the body, offered in the fire, is to become ashes («अथ इदं शरीरमग्नौ हुतं भस्मान्तं भस्मावशेषं भूयात्»). He infers the subtle body’s going out from the fact that a path is asked for in the next mantra. Mahīdhara gives the same reading for the Mādhyandina text and adds Kātyāyana’s rule. Deśika does not read the first half as a death rite at all: it states the nature of the pure self, immortal while the body perishes.

commentary.q: What is kratu, and what does ‘remember’ ask?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: For Śaṅkara the Om stands for Brahman under the name Agni, and kratu is its epithet, ‘whose nature is resolve’: «हे क्रतो सङ्कल्पात्मक स्मर यन्मम स्मर्तव्यं तस्य कालोऽयं प्रत्युपस्थितः» — ‘remember what is to be remembered for me; its time has come’ — and ‘remember the works I have done since childhood’. For Deśika kratu is the Lord as sacrifice, and to remember is to regard the devotee with grace («सानुग्रहया बुद्ध्या विषयीकुरु»); he cites the Gītā’s ‘I am the kratu, I am the sacrifice’ (9.16) and the Chāndogya’s ‘a person is made of kratu’. Madhva, citing verses he attributes to the Brahmatarka, insists that the Lord’s ‘remembering’ is not an act of recall, since his knowledge is eternal, but his turning towards grace («अनुग्रहोन्मुखत्वं तु»).

commentary.q: What is the grammar of the first half?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: vāyur anilam amṛtam has a nominative, then two words that can be masculine accusatives or neuter nominatives. If accusative, a verb of going must be supplied: ‘breath [goes to] the immortal air’ — Śaṅkara’s «प्रतिपद्यताम्» is such a supplement, which he labels «वाक्यशेषः», ‘the remainder of the sentence’. If nominative, the three words are predicates of one subject, as Deśika reads them. atha idaṃ bhasmāntaṃ śarīram is a nominal sentence whichever way the first is taken. The Kāṇva Saṃhitā and the Mādhyandina witness both write ‘om’ with the pluti figure (ओम्३, ओ३म्): the syllable is prolonged in recitation.

advaita.text: The dying meditator wishes that the breath return to the cosmic air, the subtle body go out, and the body become ashes in the fire; he then asks Agni, called Om and kratu, to remember what he has meditated on and done, for ‘the time has come’. The repetition expresses earnestness («क्रतो स्मर कृतं स्मर इति पुनर्वचनमादरार्थम्»). The prayer belongs to the path of meditation and works, not to the knowledge of mantra 7.

visistadvaita.text: The first half distinguishes the self from the body: the pure self is vāyu, anila and amṛta, immortal while the body ends in ashes («अनन्तरं तु परिशुद्धात्मस्वरूपमुच्यते»); then Om names the Supreme Person, the controller, completing the triad of enjoyer, enjoyed and impeller. kratu is the Lord as sacrifice, and ‘remember what has been done’ asks him, who is grateful, to protect the devotee for whatever service he has done («मत्कृतं यत्किञ्चिदनुकूलमनुसन्धाय कृतज्ञस्त्वं मां रक्षेति भावः»).

dvaita.text: Madhva’s cited verses take anila as ‘whose abode is Brahman’ («अः ब्रह्मैव निलयनं यस्य वायोः सोऽनिलम्») and make Vāyu immortal because his knowledge is never obscured; kratu and Agni are names of Hari («स क्रतुर्ज्ञानरूपत्वादग्निरङ्गप्रणेतृतः»); and the Lord’s ‘remembering’ of his devotees is his turning to them in grace, not recollection. Madhva cites these verses from texts he names (Brahmāṇḍa, Rāmasaṃhitā, Brahmatarka); the edition reports them as cited by him.

schools.disagreement: The first half is a death rite for Śaṅkara and Mahīdhara and a statement about the self for Deśika; kratu is Agni-Brahman as resolve (Śaṅkara), the Lord as sacrifice (Deśika), or a name of Hari (Madhva); and the deeds to be remembered are the dying person’s works (Śaṅkara) or the devotee’s service seen with grace (Deśika, Madhva).

parallels.note: The same mantra in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka’s closing prayer (Kāṇva), in the same place among the four.
‘A person is made of resolve (kratu); as his resolve is in this world, so he becomes on departing.’ The doctrine that gives weight to a resolve at death; Deśika alludes to this passage.

parallels.quote: यं यं वापि स्मरन्भावं त्यजत्यन्ते कलेबरम्
parallels.note: Whatever state one remembers when leaving the body at the end, to that one goes. The Gītā develops the same link between remembering and the moment of death.
‘I am the kratu, I am the sacrifice.’ Deśika cites it to explain the vocative krato as the Lord in the form of the sacrifice.

contemporary.text: Much modern discussion of death avoids its physical facts. This mantra states them flatly — breath to air, body to ashes — and then turns to what a life has been for. People who sit with the dying often describe something like the mantra’s second half: a gathering of attention, a reviewing of what was done, a wish to be remembered rightly. The mantra suggests that facing the end of the body plainly and caring about what one has done are not in tension. This is a reflection on the teaching, not part of the commentaries.

reflect.beginner: If you had to tell someone, in one sentence, what you have done that you would most like remembered, what would you say?
reflect.deeper: What in a person ‘remembers’ at the end — and is the one who is asked to remember outside us, within us, or both?
reflect.practice: At the end of a day, sit quietly for five minutes and recall what you did, from morning to evening, without judging. Close by naming one thing you would like to carry into tomorrow.

references.text: Mahīdhara (on VS 40.15) gives the viniyoga of Om: «अस्य ब्रह्म ऋषिः गायत्रीच्छन्दः परमात्मा देवता».

flags.note: The verb of the first half is supplied by the commentators; the edition’s readable rendering follows Śaṅkara’s supplement and says so in ‘Syntax’.
The sense of the Mādhyandina klibe is known here only through Mahīdhara’s derivation.
